name: Noir B&W
direction:
Aesthetic directives

BLACK-AND-WHITE FILM NOIR — 1940s-50s. Every shot must embody all of these simultaneously.

TONAL STRUCTURE. This is true black-and-white photography with no color information whatsoever. Blacks are crushed to pure, flat black with no detail retained in shadows. Highlights are blown or held at the very edge of clipping. Midtones are sparse and compressed — most of the frame lives in the extremes. Contrast is global and brutal. The tonal range is narrow and hard, not graduated.

LIGHT LOGIC. Lighting is hard, practical, and motivated. Use Fresnel spotlights with sharp falloff. Every light source is either visible in frame or clearly implied by the direction of shadows. Key lights are hard and directional. Fill is minimal or absent — let shadows go black. Backlight catches edges and smoke. No soft ambient wash. No neon. No colored lighting. Light is depicted, not implied.

CHIAROSCURO AND SHADOW. Shadow is the primary compositional element. Use hard-edged shadows from practical objects: venetian blinds, fire escapes, stair rails, door frames, hat brims. Shadows are sharp, defined, and geometric. They divide the frame into zones of visibility and concealment. A face half in shadow is the default state.

SURFACE. This is 35mm celluloid film. Visible grain, fine and constant. Not digital noise, not film stock from the 1970s. The grain is the physical texture of silver halide crystals. It shimmers slightly with motion but does not pulse or migrate. No digital smoothing. No HDR flattening.

EDGE BEHAVIOR. Forms terminate with hard edges where they meet light, and dissolve into pure black where they meet shadow. There is no gradient between lit and unlit — the transition is sharp. Outlines are absent. Halation is minimal unless a practical light source is in frame.

DEPTH STRATEGY. Deep focus is preferred. Use wide-angle lenses at small apertures to keep foreground and background both sharp. Depth is carried by overlapping planes and atmospheric haze from smoke or fog. The image reads as a window into a three-dimensional space with hard planes of light and dark.

COMPOSITION GRAMMAR. Low angles are common. Dutch tilts are permitted but not default. Frames are often entered from an edge rather than built from the centre. Mass sits asymmetrically. The ratio of empty dark area to occupied lit area is high — darkness dominates the frame. Framing devices like doorways, windows, and stairwells are used to compress space.

PROVENANCE MARKERS. This is aged film stock. Include subtle film scratches, occasional dust or hair in the gate, and a slight flicker in exposure. The image has a history as a physical object that was projected many times. No digital cleanliness.

MOTION IMPLICATION. Grain shimmers constantly at a fine scale. Smoke and fog drift slowly. Light sources flicker with the instability of practical electricity. Shadows move hard and fast when the light source moves. There is no motion blur on the film itself — only the natural motion of subjects and camera.

ANTI-TROPE MANDATE (critical).

Strictly avoid the AI video tropes that ruin authentic noir:
- NO neon lighting. No neon colors. No cyan, magenta, or electric blue.
- NO glowing eyes, glowing objects, or bioluminescence.
- NO soft ambient washes or gradient lighting.
- NO modern digital grading with lifted blacks or teal-orange color cast.
- NO rim lighting for beauty. Edges are lit only when motivated by a practical backlight.
- NO digital noise that pulses or migrates. Grain is fine, constant, and physical.
- Keep lighting grounded in practical sources: desk lamps, street lamps, overhead fixtures, windows, candles.

CAMERA AND FRAMING.

The supplied `camera` string is the authoritative motion — use it as written. Layer the noir flavor around it: hard shadows that track with the light source, deep focus planes that remain sharp, the slight instability of a heavy 1940s camera dolly or tripod. Do not write cut or transition language.

SUBJECT RIGGING (critical).

Describe the physical state of the subject's face and mouth explicitly, using the supplied `rigging` value. Every subject in every shot needs one. Always end the rigging clause with exactly:
to prevent any facial babbling or lip-sync hallucinations.

PRACTICAL EFFECTS AND COSTUME.

Costume is a textural element. Trench coats, fedoras, shoulder pads, silk, wool, damp fabric. These materials interact with hard light to create sharp highlights and deep folds. Include the supplied `practical_effects` value. Lighting is hard and directional. Texture note: the materials must read as physical fabric or solid surface, not rendered.

AUDIO.

`overall_soundscape` — the physical, diegetic sounds only. Rain on pavement, distant traffic, footsteps on wet asphalt, a door closing, the hum of a practical light, fabric movement, breathing. Write this richly.

`non_diegetic_music` — always exactly `N/A`.

Do not write "Audio:", "Director's note:", "Storyboard:", or any timestamp bracket notation.

CONTENT BOUNDARY.

All human characters are fictional adults. Human characters are fully clothed in opaque clothing. No nudity, sexual imagery, explicit sexual content, real-person likenesses, blood or gore. Animals and other non-human subjects are depicted non-sexually.
style_card: Authentic 1940s-50s black-and-white film noir. High-contrast chiaroscuro, hard practical lighting, 35mm celluloid grain.
